title: Speak with Flow: The Speaking Framework
subtitle: A practical guide to the IELTS Speaking test, from Part 1 answers to natural rhythm
description: This ebook explains how Speaking is scored and gives clear methods for Part 1, Part 2 and Part 3. It also helps you reduce fillers and improve pronunciation and rhythm with a four-week plan.
audience: Bangladeshi IELTS learners at about Band 5 to 6 who want longer, smoother and clearer Speaking answers.

chapters.title: How the Speaking Test Works and How It Is Scored
chapters.summary: Learn the shape of the test and the four criteria the examiner uses to give your band.
chapters.body:
The IELTS Speaking test is a face-to-face conversation with one examiner. It lasts 11 to 14 minutes and has three parts. The examiner records the test. Nobody is trying to trick you. The examiner wants to hear how well you can use English to communicate.

## The three parts

- Part 1 is an introduction and interview. The examiner checks your identity and asks short questions about familiar topics such as home, work, study, food or free time. This part is usually about four to five minutes.
- Part 2 is the long turn. You get a task card, one minute to prepare, and then you speak for up to two minutes. The examiner may ask one or two short questions afterwards.
- Part 3 is a discussion. The examiner asks more abstract questions linked to the Part 2 topic. This part is also usually about four to five minutes.

## The four criteria

Your Speaking band comes from four criteria. They are equally weighted, so each one matters the same amount.

- Fluency and Coherence: Can you keep going without long pauses, and are your ideas easy to follow?
- Lexical Resource: Do you have enough words to talk about many topics, and can you paraphrase when you forget a word?
- Grammatical Range and Accuracy: Do you use a mix of simple and complex sentences, and how often do errors get in the way?
- Pronunciation: Can the examiner understand you easily? Do you use stress, rhythm and intonation in a natural way?

Notice what is not on the list. The examiner does not score your ideas for being clever or true. You can invent a holiday you never took. You will not lose marks for a boring opinion. You will lose marks for silence, for very short answers and for speech that is hard to follow.

## What this means for Band 5 to 6 learners

At Band 5, many learners can speak, but they pause often to search for words, repeat the same simple words and give short answers. At Band 6, speakers can talk at some length, although they may still hesitate sometimes and make errors. The big step is not perfect English. It is steady, connected speech with a little more range.

So your first goal is simple: say more, say it in connected sentences, and keep the examiner able to follow you.

Example: The examiner asks, "Do you like cooking?" A short answer is "Yes." A stronger answer is "Yes, I do, mostly at the weekend. My mother taught me how to make beef bhuna, and now I cook it for my cousins when they visit."

## Habits to build from today

Speak English aloud every day, even for five minutes. Reading in your head does not train your mouth. Record yourself on your phone and listen back. You will hear pauses, fillers and unclear words that you cannot notice while speaking.

Also, treat the test as a conversation, not an exam. Look at the examiner, smile a little, and answer as if a new colleague asked you a friendly question.

Tip: If you do not understand a question, it is fine to ask the examiner to repeat it. Say, "Sorry, could you say that again, please?" Do not overuse this, but it is far better than guessing and speaking about the wrong thing.

In the next chapters you will practise one skill at a time: extending Part 1 answers, using the Part 2 minute, telling a story, building Part 3 opinions, controlling fillers, and finding a natural rhythm.
takeaways: The test has three parts and takes 11 to 14 minutes.
Four equally weighted criteria decide your band: Fluency and Coherence, Lexical Resource, Grammatical Range and Accuracy, and Pronunciation.
The examiner scores your English, not the truth or cleverness of your ideas.
Connected speech matters more than perfect speech.
chapters.exercise: Record yourself answering, 'Tell me about your hometown,' for one minute. Listen once and write down how many long pauses and one-word answers you hear.

chapters.title: Part 1: Giving Extended Answers
chapters.summary: Turn short replies into two or three connected sentences without sounding memorised.
chapters.body:
Part 1 is your warm-up, but it is also where many candidates lose marks. They give very short answers, and the examiner cannot hear enough language to judge. The fix is to learn a simple answer shape and use it again and again.

## The answer, reason, example shape

For most Part 1 questions, aim for two or three sentences. Use this pattern:

- Answer the question directly.
- Add a reason or detail.
- Give a small example or a personal fact.

You do not need to give a long speech. Part 1 questions are quick, and the examiner moves on. Two good sentences are better than one word, and three are better than one rambling paragraph.

Example: Question: "Do you often use public transport?" Answer: "Yes, I take a bus almost every day because driving in Dhaka is too stressful. Last week the traffic near Farmgate was so bad that my journey took nearly two hours, so I now leave home earlier."

## Add a small story or a contrast

Two easy ways to extend are contrast and time. For contrast, say what used to be true: "I didn't like tea before, but now I drink it every evening." For time, mention a recent event or a plan: "I'm hoping to visit Cox's Bazar next winter."

Linking words help you keep going smoothly. Useful ones for Part 1 are because, so, but, although, and, for example, and these days.

## Do not memorise full answers

Many learners learn answers by heart. Examiners are trained to notice this, and memorised speech often sounds flat, too fast or unrelated to the question. Instead, prepare ideas and a few flexible phrases. Think about your own life: your family, your studies or job, your area, your favourite food, your phone use, your weekends. If you have things to say about ten topics, you can handle almost any Part 1 question.

## Handling topics you do not like

Sometimes the topic feels boring, such as "Do you like flowers?" Be honest but add a reason. "Not really, because I'm allergic to pollen, but I enjoy seeing roses at weddings." You can also talk about people you know: "My aunt grows flowers on her roof in Chattogram, and she's really proud of them."

If you have never done something, say so and explain. "I've never been to a museum, to be honest, but I'd like to visit the National Museum because I've heard it has a lot of history."

## Keep it natural

Use short natural openers such as "Well," "Actually," "To be honest," or "That's an interesting question." Use them lightly. One in every few answers is enough.

Tip: Practise with a timer. Answer each question in about 15 to 25 seconds. If you finish in five seconds, add a reason. If you are still talking after 40 seconds, finish your sentence and stop.

Finally, stay relaxed about grammar. Choose sentences you can control. A clear sentence with a small error is better than a complicated sentence that you abandon halfway.
takeaways: Aim for two or three sentences: answer, reason, example.
Use contrast or time, such as used to and these days, to add detail.
Prepare ideas and flexible phrases, not memorised paragraphs.
If you have never done something, say so and explain why.
chapters.exercise: Choose five Part 1 topics from your own life. For each, write one question and answer it aloud in 15 to 25 seconds using answer, reason, example.

chapters.title: Part 2: Structuring Your Long Turn and Using the Minute
chapters.summary: Use the one-minute preparation time to build a simple plan and speak for nearly two minutes.
chapters.body:
Part 2 frightens many learners because you must speak alone for up to two minutes. The good news is that you receive a task card with bullet points and one minute to prepare. If you use that minute well, the talk becomes much easier.

## What happens

The examiner gives you a card, a pencil and paper. You have one minute to prepare. Then you speak for up to two minutes. The examiner will stop you when time is up. Aim to reach close to the two minutes, because a very short talk gives the examiner less language to score.

## Do not write sentences

One minute is very short. If you try to write full sentences, you will run out of time and then read them badly. Instead, write keywords only. Use a simple grid:

- Beginning: what and who (one or two words)
- Middle: two or three key points (single words)
- End: feeling or result (one word)

Example: Card: "Describe a festival you enjoy." Notes: Eid / family / new clothes / cooking / visiting / happy, tired.

## Use the card as your map

The card usually has four prompts. They are your outline. Speak about them in order. If the card asks what the festival is, when it happens, what people do and why you like it, then you already have four paragraphs. Give each prompt around 25 to 30 seconds.

## A simple structure

Open with one sentence that answers the card: "I'd like to talk about Eid-ul-Fitr, which is my favourite festival." Then move through the prompts. End with a closing line: "So that's why this festival means so much to me."

Useful signposts include: "To begin with," "After that," "What I enjoy most is," and "All in all." They help the examiner follow you and give you time to think.

## What if you run out of things to say?

This is the most common fear. Have a rescue plan:

- Add a detail: colours, sounds, smells, weather.
- Add a feeling: how you felt then and how you feel now.
- Add a comparison: how it is different from the past.
- Add a person: what your friend or relative said or did.

If you finish your points early, say, "Another thing I should mention is..." and add one rescue detail.

## What if the topic is unfamiliar?

You do not have to tell the truth. If you have never visited a famous building, choose a place you know and describe it, or invent one. The examiner scores language, not facts. Just do not spend your minute inventing; pick something quickly.

Tip: In your notes, write the first word of each prompt as a column. Your eyes can jump down the page while you speak. Do not look at the paper the whole time. Glance at it, then look up.

Practise with a timer at home. Many learners find that two minutes feels longer than they expect. Do it five times with different cards, and you will start to feel the length.
takeaways: Use the one minute to write keywords only, not sentences.
Follow the prompts on the card in order as your outline.
Aim to speak for close to two minutes.
Keep rescue ideas ready: details, feelings, comparisons and people.
chapters.exercise: Take a card such as 'Describe a person who helped you.' Spend exactly one minute making keyword notes, then speak for two minutes with a timer.

chapters.title: Part 2: Storytelling and Description
chapters.summary: Make your long turn vivid with a clear timeline, sensory detail and personal feeling.
chapters.body:
Most Part 2 cards ask you to describe a person, place, object or event. Many ask you to tell a story. Good storytelling makes your speech easier to follow and gives you natural chances to use varied grammar and vocabulary.

## Tell it in order

A story needs a simple timeline. Use past tense and time markers to move forward:

- First, one day, at the beginning
- Then, after a while, soon afterwards
- Suddenly, just as, by the time
- In the end, eventually, looking back

Example: "Last year, during a long load-shedding evening, my whole family sat on the roof. At first we were annoyed, but then my uncle started telling stories from his village. After a while, we forgot about the heat altogether."

Notice that this small example has a place, a problem, a change and a feeling. That is a complete mini story.

## Describe with your senses

For people, places and objects, do not list facts only. Add what you can see, hear, smell or feel. Instead of "The market is big," say, "The market is crowded and noisy, and you can smell fresh fish and spices from every corner." Sensory detail makes speech sound natural, and it gives you language to use without needing rare words.

## Use a description frame

When you describe a person or place, try this order:

- What it is, and where or when
- What it looks like or what the person is like
- A specific memory or example
- Why it matters to you

For a person, move from appearance to character to a moment. "My teacher is tall and always wears a plain cotton shirt. She is patient and funny. Once, when I failed a test, she stayed after class to explain every mistake."

## Give your feelings

Examiners listen for personal language. Phrases like "I felt proud," "I was a bit nervous," "It reminded me of..." and "What I remember most is..." show that you are talking, not reciting. Feelings also help you fill the second minute.

## Grammar that comes naturally in stories

You do not need to force advanced grammar. Stories bring it up on their own:

- Past simple and past continuous: "I was walking home when it started to rain."
- Past perfect for earlier events: "By the time I arrived, the programme had already started."
- Used to for habits: "We used to visit my grandparents every Friday."
- Simple comparisons: "It was much quieter than I expected."

Tip: When you tell a past story, check your tense. Many learners start in the past and slip into the present. Say the first verb of every new sentence slowly in your head until the habit is automatic.

## Paraphrase when words fail

If you forget a word, explain it. "I can't remember the word, but it's the small machine you use to cool a room" is perfectly acceptable. Paraphrasing shows Lexical Resource skills. Do not freeze.

Practise by telling the same story three times. The first time, use basic words. The second, add sensory details. The third, add feelings and one comparison. You will notice the story grows richer without becoming harder.
takeaways: Use a clear timeline with time markers such as first, then and in the end.
Add sensory detail and personal feeling to make descriptions vivid.
Past tenses and used to appear naturally in stories.
If you forget a word, paraphrase and keep going.
chapters.exercise: Tell a one-minute story about a time the electricity went off. Include one time marker, two sensory details and one feeling.

chapters.title: Part 3: Giving Abstract and Developed Answers
chapters.summary: Move from personal examples to opinions, reasons and comparisons about society.
chapters.body:
Part 3 is a discussion with the examiner. The questions are more abstract than in Parts 1 and 2. Instead of "Do you like festivals?" you may hear "How have festivals changed in your country?" or "Why do some people think traditions are important?" This is where examiners see whether you can handle ideas.

## What changes in Part 3

In Part 1 you talk about yourself. In Part 3 you talk about people in general, society, the past and the future. You still do not need expert knowledge. You need a clear opinion and one or two reasons.

## The opinion, reason, example, result shape

Try this pattern for most answers, usually in four to six sentences:

- Give your opinion or a direct answer.
- Explain why.
- Give an example from your country or experience.
- Add a result, a comparison, or the other side.

Example: Question: "Do you think young people spend too much time online?" Answer: "I think many of them do. Phones are cheap and data packages are easy to get, so it's tempting to scroll for hours. For example, my younger cousin often stays up until midnight watching videos, and then he's exhausted at school. On the other hand, the internet also helps students learn, so the problem is mainly balance."

## Useful language for opinions

- "In my view," "As far as I'm concerned," "I'd say that..."
- "One reason is..." "Another factor is..."
- "That depends on..." "It varies from person to person."
- "On the one hand... on the other hand..."
- "I tend to think..." "I'm not entirely sure, but I suppose..."

Notice that some phrases soften your opinion. That is natural. Real people often say "It depends" and then explain.

## Handling questions about the past and future

Part 3 often asks you to compare then and now, or to predict. For the past, use "In the past, people used to... but nowadays..." For the future, use "I think it will probably..." or "In ten years, I expect..." Do not worry about perfect grammar. Aim for clear, calm sentences.

## When you have no idea

If you have never thought about the question, buy time politely: "That's a tricky question. Let me think for a moment." Then pick a simple angle. Think about who is affected: children, workers, parents, the government. Or think about money, time, health, or technology. These angles give you something to say about almost anything.

## Do not give a lecture

Keep each answer under about 40 seconds. The examiner may ask a follow-up, and you want a conversation. If you have said your opinion, reason and example, you can stop. A pause after a complete answer is not a problem.

Tip: Avoid the answer "Yes, it is good" with nothing else. Always add a "because" or "for example." Use it as a reflex.

To build this skill, listen to a short news item or read a short article in English. Then ask yourself a general question about it and answer in four to six sentences. Do this three times a week.
takeaways: Part 3 asks about people in general, society, the past and the future.
Use opinion, reason, example and result to build developed answers.
Softening phrases such as it depends are natural and acceptable.
If an idea is hard, use angles: people, money, time, health or technology.
chapters.exercise: Answer aloud: 'Why do some people prefer living in big cities?' Use opinion, reason, example and result, and keep it under 40 seconds.

chapters.title: Fluency and Fillers: Speaking Smoothly Without Silence
chapters.summary: Reduce long pauses and distracting fillers while keeping your speech natural and connected.
chapters.body:
Fluency does not mean speaking fast. It means speaking with a steady flow and without long, frequent breaks to search for words or grammar. Coherence means your ideas link together so that the listener can follow. Together they make up one of the four criteria.

## Pausing is normal

Native speakers pause to think. A short pause at the end of an idea is natural and even helpful. The problem is long pauses in the middle of sentences, repeated restarts, and sounds like "uhhh" that fill every gap. Your goal is to move pauses to the right places: between ideas, not inside them.

## Fillers: use them smartly

Fillers are small sounds and phrases such as "um," "uh," "you know," "like" and "I mean." Everyone uses some. Too many make speech tiring and unclear.

Replace the empty sound with a short thinking phrase:

- "Let me think..."
- "Well, I suppose..."
- "That's a good question."
- "How can I put it?"
- "What I mean is..."

These phrases give you two or three seconds to plan. They sound more controlled than a long "ummm." But do not use them in every answer. Once or twice in a few answers is enough.

## Do not repeat and restart

Another fluency problem is false starts: "I think... I think... I think the city is..." If you notice this, practise finishing the sentence you started, even if it is imperfect. A small grammar error costs less than a stop-start rhythm. Self-correction is fine when it is occasional: "He go... he goes to work early." One quick fix is natural. Constant fixing is not.

## Practise speaking in chunks

Fluent speakers do not build every sentence word by word. They use chunks, which are phrases that come together as a unit. Examples: "to be honest," "a lot of people," "as far as I know," "it depends on," "in the end," "I'm looking forward to." Learn five new chunks each week and use them in real speech.

## Connect ideas with simple links

You do not need rare linkers. Use because, so, but, and, then, for example, also, however and in addition. Repeating "and then" in a story is acceptable if your pronunciation and rhythm are clear, but try to add variety.

## Training exercises

- Shadowing: Play a short clip of a speaker, then repeat it right after the speaker, copying the speed and pauses.
- Timed talking: Choose a topic and speak for one minute without stopping. If you get stuck, use a thinking phrase and move on.
- Record and count: Record yourself, then count fillers per minute. Aim to reduce the number each week.

Tip: When you cannot find a word, do not go silent. Use a general word and add detail: "a kind of vehicle with three wheels" for a CNG. The examiner values communication.

Remember that anxiety makes pauses longer. Breathe slowly before you answer. A calm start usually leads to smoother speech.
takeaways: Fluency means steady flow, not fast speech.
Replace empty fillers with short thinking phrases, and use them sparingly.
Finish sentences instead of repeatedly restarting them.
Learn and reuse chunks of language to speak more smoothly.
chapters.exercise: Record one minute on 'my daily routine.' Count how many times you say um, uh or like, and try again to reduce that number.

chapters.title: Pronunciation, Natural Rhythm and Your Revision Plan
chapters.summary: Improve stress, rhythm and clarity for Bangladeshi speakers, then follow a four-week plan to revise everything.
chapters.body:
Pronunciation is one criterion, and it is about being understood easily. You do not need an American or British accent. You need clear sounds, good word stress, natural rhythm and helpful intonation. Learners from Bangladesh often speak Bangla with a rhythm that gives each syllable roughly equal weight. English works differently, and that is the key to sounding natural.

## Stress and rhythm

English words have a stressed syllable. Say "PHOtograph," "phoTOgrapher," "photoGRAPHic." Wrong word stress can make a word hard to recognise. Check stress in a dictionary and mark it when you learn new words.

In sentences, English stresses content words (nouns, main verbs, adjectives) and shortens small words (to, of, and, can). Compare "I want to GO to the MARket" with a flat, even version. Practise clapping on the stressed words.

## Sounds that often need attention

Every learner is different, so record yourself. These areas are common to check:

- Words that begin with s plus a consonant, such as school, station and street. Some speakers add a vowel before them. Practise "school," not "ischool."
- Final consonants. Do not drop the endings of words like asked, helped or months. Final sounds often carry grammar.
- The sounds in think and this, and the difference between w and v.
- Long and short vowels, such as ship and sheep.

Choose one or two problems at a time. Do not try to fix everything at once.

## Intonation

Your voice should move. A flat voice sounds uninterested, and the examiner may find it hard to hear what is important. Let your voice rise a little on new ideas and fall at the end of a finished statement. Use a slightly stronger voice on the key word: "I really enjoyed it."

## Speak clearly, not fast

Under stress, many candidates speed up and swallow sounds. Slow down by about ten percent and open your mouth slightly more. Clarity is better than speed.

## Your four-week revision plan

- Week 1: Learn the test structure and four criteria. Record Part 1 answers daily and use answer, reason, example.
- Week 2: Practise Part 2 with one-minute keyword notes. Do two timed talks a day with a story and sensory detail.
- Week 3: Practise Part 3 with opinion, reason, example and result. Learn five chunks and reduce fillers.
- Week 4: Do two full mock tests with a friend or teacher, record them, and review pronunciation, fluency and grammar errors.

Tip: Listen to your recordings the next day, not immediately. You will notice problems more clearly with fresh ears.

Keep a small notebook of three mistakes you repeat. Check it before each practice. Steady daily speaking, even for ten minutes, will help more than one long session each week.
takeaways: Stress content words and shorten small words for natural rhythm.
Pick one or two sound problems at a time and record yourself.
Slow down slightly and finish word endings for clarity.
Follow a four-week plan and review recordings the next day.
chapters.exercise: Choose one pronunciation problem and record five sentences containing it. Listen the next day and note one thing to fix in your four-week plan.
